The project team shall be structured to provide clear lines of responsibility and communication. The key roles and responsibilities are defined below:

- **Project Director:** Owns the overall delivery of the project, chairs the PCG, and reports to the Project Board.
- **Project Manager:** Manages the day-to-day delivery, coordinates the Delivery Team, and manages the project controls function.
- **Lead Engineer:** Manages the engineering design, technical assurance, and integration of the design with the construction activities.
- **Construction Manager:** Manages all site-based activities, including health, safety, and environmental (HSE) performance, quality assurance, and the management of the principal contractor.
- **Project Controls Manager:** Manages the planning, cost, and risk functions, providing the data necessary for informed decision-making.
- **Procurement Manager:** Manages all procurement activities, including the tendering and award of subcontracts and the management of the supply chain.

**3.2 Stakeholder Management**

Effective stakeholder engagement is critical to the success of Project X. A Stakeholder Matrix has been developed and is maintained by the PMO, identifying all internal and external stakeholders, their level of interest and influence, and the communication strategy for each. The matrix is reviewed at each PCG meeting.

Key stakeholders include:

- **Sponsoring Organisation:** The parent company funding the project.
- **Client/End Users:** The team who will operate the facility upon completion.
- **Local Authority:** Leeds City Council, with responsibility for planning and building control.
- **Regulatory Bodies:** Environment Agency, Health and Safety Executive (HSE).
- **Local Community:** Residents and businesses adjacent to the Northbridge Industrial Estate.
- **Principal Contractor:** The tier-one contractor responsible for the construction works.
- **Supply Chain:** Subcontractors and material suppliers.

**4. SCOPE MANAGEMENT**

**4.1 Scope Definition**

The scope of Project X is defined in the Project Execution Plan (PEP-PX-003) and the associated technical specifications and drawings. Any work not explicitly defined in these documents is considered to be out of scope.

**4.2 Scope Change Control**

All changes to the project scope shall be managed through the formal Change Control Procedure (see Section 7 of this document). No work outside the defined scope shall be undertaken without an approved Change Request.

**5. SCHEDULE MANAGEMENT**

**5.1 Baseline Schedule**

The project baseline schedule is defined in the Level 3 Programme, reference SCH-PX-004, Revision B. The schedule is based on a contract duration of 35 months, with a planned completion date of 30 November 2027.

Key milestone dates are as follows:

- **Project Start (NTP):** 13 January 2025
- **Design Freeze:** 30 June 2025
- **Construction Start:** 01 September 2025
- **Mechanical Completion:** 30 June 2027
- **Commissioning & Handover:** 30 November 2027

**5.2 Schedule Control**

Progress will be monitored against the baseline schedule on a weekly basis. Earned Value Management (EVM) will be used to measure schedule performance, with Schedule Performance Index (SPI) and Cost Performance Index (CPI) reported to the PCG monthly. Any variance requiring corrective action will be managed through the Risk and Issue Management process.

**6. BUDGET AND COST MANAGEMENT**

**6.1 Budget Baseline**

The Project Management Plan states that Project X has_budget 250000000 GBP. Record status: current. This figure represents the current approved budget baseline, inclusive of all direct and indirect costs, risk allowance, and contingency.
**7.1 General**

All changes to the project scope, schedule, budget, or quality requirements shall be managed through the Change Control Procedure. The purpose of this procedure is to ensure that all changes are assessed for their impact on the project objectives and that approved changes are implemented in a controlled manner.

**7.2 Change Request Submission**

Any stakeholder, contractor, or member of the project team may submit a Change Request using the standard form (CR-PX-001). The form shall be submitted to the Project Management Office (PMO) for logging and initial review. The Change Request shall include:

- A description of the proposed change.
- The reason for the change.
- An assessment of the impact on scope, schedule, budget, and quality.
- Any supporting documentation, such as drawings, specifications, or quotations.

**7.3 Change Request Review**

The PMO shall review each Change Request within five working days of receipt. The review shall include an assessment of the technical feasibility, the impact on the baseline, and the risks associated with the change. The PMO shall then submit the Change Request to the Change Control Board (CCB) for decision.

**7.4 Change Control Board**

The CCB shall comprise the following members:

- Project Sponsor (Chair)
- Project Director
- Head of Project Controls
- Head of Engineering
- Head of Construction
- Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) Manager

The CCB shall meet on a weekly basis, or more frequently if required, to review and approve or reject Change Requests. The CCB shall consider the impact of each change on the project objectives, the risk profile, and the overall value for money. The decision of the CCB shall be recorded in the minutes of the meeting and communicated to the applicant within two working days.

According to the Project Management Plan, Site Alpha has_planned_completion 2026-03-31. Record status: current.

**7.5 Implementation of Approved Changes**

Once a Change Request has been approved, the PMO shall update the relevant project documentation, including the scope definition, schedule, budget, and risk register. The change shall be communicated to all affected parties, and the project team shall implement the change in accordance with the approved plan. No work shall commence on a change until it has been formally approved by the CCB.

**8. QUALITY MANAGEMENT**

**8.1 Quality Policy**

The quality policy for Project X is to deliver a facility that meets the requirements defined in the technical specifications and the associated British and European standards. The project shall operate a quality management system (QMS) in accordance with ISO 9001:2015, as adapted for the construction industry.

**8.2 Quality Assurance and Quality Control**

Quality assurance (QA) activities shall be undertaken to ensure that the processes used to deliver the project are appropriate and effective. Quality control (QC) activities shall be undertaken to ensure that the products and works meet the specified requirements.

The principal contractor shall be responsible for the development and implementation of a Project Quality Plan (PQP), which shall be submitted to the PMO for approval prior to the commencement of construction works. The PQP shall include:

- The organisational structure and responsibilities for quality.
- Procedures for the control of documents and records.
- Procedures for inspection and testing.
- Procedures for the management of nonconformances.
- Procedures for internal audit.

The PMO shall undertake regular audits of the principal contractor's quality management system and shall monitor the implementation of the PQP throughout the construction phase.
A nonconformance shall be recorded whenever a product, material, or workmanship does not meet the specified requirements. The principal contractor shall maintain a nonconformance register and shall issue a Nonconformance Report (NCR) to the PMO within two working days of identification. Each NCR shall include:

- A unique reference number and the date of identification.
- The location and the relevant work package.
- A description of the nonconformance and the suspected cause.
- The proposed disposition (rework, repair, use-as-is, or reject).
- The signature of the responsible engineer.

The PMO shall review each NCR and shall approve or reject the proposed disposition within five working days. Where the disposition is use-as-is, the PMO shall obtain the written agreement of the client. All costs arising from a nonconformance shall be borne by the party responsible, as determined by the contract.

**8.5 Internal Audit**

The PMO shall undertake internal audits of the project management system and of the principal contractor's quality management system at intervals of not more than three months. Audit findings shall be classified as major nonconformances, minor nonconformances, or observations. Corrective action plans shall be submitted to the PMO within ten working days of the audit report being issued.

**9. SCHEDULE MANAGEMENT**

**9.1 Schedule Baseline**

The project schedule baseline is shown in the Project Programme, which is maintained by the PMO and issued as a controlled document. The schedule is prepared using the precedence diagramming method and is expressed in working days. The baseline programme for the overall project shows the planned completion date for the entire Project X scope as 2026-09-30. Within that overall programme, the two principal site packages have their own completion targets, which are recorded as controlled schedule milestones.

The Project Management Plan records that Site Beta has_planned_completion 2026-06-30. Record status: current. This date is the contractual completion date for the Site Beta package and is subject to change only through the formal change control procedure described in Section 7.

**9.2 Schedule Control**

The principal contractor shall provide a monthly progress report to the PMO, showing the planned versus actual progress for each work package, together with an updated programme. The monthly report shall include:

- A narrative summary of progress, including any issues affecting the programme.
- A comparison of planned versus actual start and completion dates for each activity.
- A list of activities completed in the reporting period.
- A forecast of activities to commence in the next two reporting periods.
- A statement of any float consumed or gained.

The PMO shall review the monthly progress report and shall advise the principal contractor of any corrective actions required. Where an activity is forecast to complete later than its planned completion date, the principal contractor shall submit a recovery plan within ten working days.

**9.3 Key Milestones for Site Beta**

The key milestones for the Site Beta package are identified in the table below. These milestones are controlled items and shall be reported against in the monthly progress report.

| SB-700 | Completion of internal finishes and commissioning | 2026-06-19 |
| SB-800 | Site Beta practical completion | 2026-06-30 |
**10. Risk Management**

**10.1 Approach**

Risk management for Project X shall be conducted in accordance with the requirements of the Project Risk Management Plan (PRMP-001) and the client's procedures for the management of project risk. The objective of the risk management process is to identify, assess, and manage uncertainties that could affect the delivery of the project objectives, including time, cost, quality, and safety.

The risk management process shall be applied throughout the project lifecycle, from initiation through to close-out. The process shall be proactive, with risks identified and assessed at the earliest opportunity, and shall be reviewed at regular intervals to reflect changes in the project environment.

**10.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

The Project Manager shall have overall accountability for the management of risk on the project. The PMO shall maintain the risk register and shall facilitate the risk review workshops. The principal contractor shall identify and manage risks associated with their scope of work and shall report material risks to the PMO as part of the monthly progress report.

The client's project sponsor shall be responsible for the acceptance of risks that fall outside the tolerance levels set for the project, as described in Section 10.5.

**10.3 Risk Identification and Assessment**

Risks shall be identified through a series of facilitated workshops, interviews, and reviews of project documentation. The initial risk identification shall be undertaken during the development of the Project Execution Plan, and shall be updated at each monthly risk review meeting.

Each risk shall be assessed against two criteria: the likelihood of occurrence and the potential impact on the project objectives. The assessment shall be recorded using the probability-impact matrix shown in Table 10-1.

*Table 10-1: Probability-Impact Matrix*

| Likelihood | Impact | Score | Classification |
|------------|--------|-------|----------------|
| Very Low | Negligible | 1 | Low |
| Low | Minor | 2 | Low |
| Medium | Moderate | 3 | Medium |
| High | Major | 4 | High |
| Very High | Severe | 5 | High |

A risk score shall be calculated by multiplying the likelihood score by the impact score. Risks with a score of 15 or above shall be classified as high risk and shall be subject to active management and mitigation. Risks with a score between 8 and 14 shall be classified as medium risk and shall be managed through the application of standard controls. Risks with a score of 7 or below shall be classified as low risk and shall be monitored through the risk register.

**10.4 Risk Response Planning**

For each risk identified, a response strategy shall be developed. The response strategy shall be selected from the following options:

- Avoid: change the project plan to eliminate the risk or protect the project objectives from its impact.
- Transfer: shift the impact of the risk to a third party, together with ownership of the response.
- Mitigate: reduce the likelihood or impact of the risk to an acceptable level.
- Accept: acknowledge the risk and document its potential impact, with no proactive action taken.

The selected response strategy shall be recorded in the risk register, together with the actions required to implement the response, the owner of the action, and the target date for completion.

**10.5 Risk Tolerances**

The project has the following risk tolerances, which shall be used to determine the level of management action required:

- A risk with a potential cost impact of more than £250,000 shall be escalated to the client's project sponsor for acceptance.
- A risk with a potential schedule impact of more than four weeks to a key milestone shall be escalated to the client's project sponsor for acceptance.
- A risk with a potential impact on the health and safety of personnel or the public shall be escalated to the client's project sponsor immediately.

Source format: Geotechnical Report

This report presents the factual and interpretive findings of the ground investigation undertaken at Site Alpha and Site Beta between 09 January 2023 and 03 February 2023. It supersedes Revision 0, issued 02 February 2023, which contained preliminary laboratory results only. This revision incorporates the complete suite of geotechnical laboratory testing and is the current controlled document for design purposes.

---

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 This report describes the ground conditions encountered at two adjacent development parcels, Site Alpha (approximately 4.2 ha) and Site Beta (approximately 2.8 ha), located near Didcot, Oxfordshire. The sites are proposed for a mixed-use development comprising residential blocks and light industrial units.

1.2 The investigation was commissioned by Meridian Infrastructure PLC under instruction number MI-4471. The purpose of the investigation was to establish the near-surface ground conditions, groundwater regime, and geotechnical parameters required for foundation design and earthworks specification.

1.3 The scope of work comprised:
- 12 no. rotary cored boreholes (BH01 to BH12)
- 8 no. window sample boreholes (WS01 to WS08)
- 6 no. trial pits (TP01 to TP06)
- In-situ testing including Standard Penetration Tests (SPT) and hand vane tests
- Installation of 4 no. standpipe piezometers
- Geotechnical laboratory testing on recovered samples

1.4 The fieldwork was carried out between 09 January and 03 February 2023. All exploratory hole positions were set out by the site surveyor, and levels were recorded relative to Ordnance Datum (m AOD).

---

2. SITE INVESTIGATION METHODS

2.1 Rotary Core Drilling

2.1.1 Boreholes BH01 to BH12 were advanced using a Dando Terrier 2000 rotary rig equipped with a 112 mm diameter core barrel. Coring was undertaken using a single tube core barrel with a tungsten carbide tipped bit. Flush returns were monitored for the presence of water, and where artesian conditions were suspected, drilling was halted and the hole was observed for a minimum of 30 minutes before continuing.

The Geotechnical Report indicates that Site Alpha has_ground_condition chalk. Record status: current.

2.1.2 Core runs were typically 1.5 m in length, with core recovery and Total Core Recovery (TCR) recorded for each run. Rock Quality Designation (RQD) was calculated for all cored runs within competent strata.

2.1.3 Upon completion of drilling, boreholes were backfilled with cement-bentonite grout, except where piezometers were installed.

2.2 Window Sampling

2.2.1 Window sample boreholes WS01 to WS08 were advanced using a window sampler rig with 1.0 m long, 100 mm diameter sample tubes. Sampling was continuous to refusal or to a maximum depth of 5.0 m.

2.2.2 SPTs were carried out at 1.0 m intervals within the window sample boreholes in accordance with BS EN ISO 22476-3:2005. The SPT hammer was a standard automatic trip hammer with a mass of 63.5 kg and a drop height of 760 mm.

2.3 Trial Pitting

2.3.1 Trial pits TP01 to TP06 were excavated using a 3-tonne mini excavator fitted with a 600 mm toothed bucket. Pits were excavated to a maximum depth of 3.0 m, with side walls inspected and logged by an engineering geologist.

2.3.2 Bulk samples for laboratory classification testing were recovered from each trial pit. In-situ hand vane tests were undertaken at 0.5 m intervals within cohesive horizons.

2.4 Groundwater Monitoring

2.4.1 Four standpipe piezometers were installed in boreholes BH02, BH05, BH08 and BH11. Each piezometer comprised a 50 mm diameter HDPE standpipe with a 1.0 m slotted response zone, surrounded by a sand filter pack and sealed with bentonite.

2.4.2 Groundwater levels were recorded at installation and subsequently on a weekly basis for a period of four weeks. The monitoring period ended on 03 March 2023.
At Site Alpha, the chalk was encountered at depths of between 1.5 m and 3.2 m bgl. The upper 0.5 m to 1.0 m of chalk was typically Grade C, becoming Grade B with increasing depth. In BH05, the chalk was encountered at 2.8 m bgl and was logged as Grade C to a depth of 6.0 m, below which it became Grade B. The chalk at Site Alpha is described in the Geotechnical Report as having a chalk grade of Grade B to C. Record status: current.

At Site Beta, the chalk was encountered at shallower depths, between 1.2 m and 2.5 m bgl. The chalk was generally of better quality than that at Site Alpha, with Grade B material recorded from the top of the chalk in BH11 and BH12. In BH13, a band of harder, Grade A chalk was recorded between 4.5 m and 5.2 m bgl.

3.5 Groundwater

3.5.1 General

Groundwater levels were recorded in the standpipe piezometers installed in BH02, BH05, BH08 and BH11 during the monitoring period between 03 February 2023 and 03 March 2023. The recorded levels are presented in Table 3.1 below. It should be noted that the monitoring period was relatively short, and that groundwater levels may vary seasonally.

Table 3.1: Groundwater levels recorded during monitoring period

Borehole | Depth to water (m bgl) | Date of reading | Notes
BH02 | 2.1 | 03 Feb 2023 | Falling
BH02 | 2.4 | 10 Feb 2023 | Falling
BH02 | 2.5 | 03 Mar 2023 | Stable
BH05 | 3.0 | 03 Feb 2023 | Rising
BH05 | 2.8 | 10 Feb 2023 | Rising
BH05 | 2.6 | 03 Mar 2023 | Stable

3.5.2 Artesian Conditions at Site Alpha

During drilling of borehole BH05 at Site Alpha, artesian water conditions were encountered. Upon completion of drilling to the full depth of 12.0 m, the borehole was observed to be flowing with water at a rate sufficient to maintain a standing water level above the ground surface. The flow was estimated at approximately 0.5 litres per second. A period of observation of 30 minutes was undertaken, during which the flow continued unabated. The artesian head was measured using a temporary standpipe and pressure gauge, which recorded a pressure equivalent to a water level of approximately 1.2 m above ground level.

The Geotechnical Report notes that Site Alpha has_ground_condition artesian water. Record status: current.

The artesian conditions are interpreted to be associated with a confined chalk aquifer beneath the site. The Head Deposits and the upper weathered chalk are considered to act as an aquitard, confining the groundwater within the more fractured and permeable chalk at depth. The artesian head is considered to be a result of the regional topography, with recharge occurring at higher elevations to the north of the site and the confined aquifer transmitting water beneath the site towards the river valley to the south.

The presence of artesian water has significant implications for the design and construction of the proposed development at Site Alpha. In particular, any excavation that penetrates the confining layer will be subject to groundwater inflow from below, which may be difficult to control. It is recommended that the following measures are considered during detailed design:

1. A full pumping test should be undertaken to determine the transmissivity and storage coefficient of the chalk aquifer, and to assess the sustainability of any dewatering scheme.

2. The design of the basement and any deep drainage should take account of the artesian head, and should incorporate appropriate pressure relief measures, such as pressure relief valves or a permanent dewatering system.

3. A permit to work should be required for any excavation that is expected to penetrate the confining layer, and a contingency plan should be in place for dealing with uncontrolled groundwater inflows.

**5.0 Recommendations for Foundation Design**

The following recommendations are made for the design of foundations for the proposed development at Site Alpha and Site Beta. These recommendations are based on the findings of the intrusive investigation, laboratory testing, and the geological model presented in Sections 2.0 to 4.0 of this report. The recommendations are made on the basis of the assumed development layout and loading, as provided by the project architects and structural engineers. Should the layout or loading change significantly, the recommendations should be reviewed.

**5.1 General**

The ground conditions across both sites are variable, and it is therefore essential that a rigorous approach to foundation design is adopted. A traditional strip or pad foundation solution is not considered appropriate for the majority of the development, due to the presence of soft, compressible Head Deposits and the potential for differential settlement. A piled foundation solution, or a ground improvement scheme, is considered necessary to transfer loads to the more competent strata.

The use of a reinforced concrete raft foundation may be considered for lightly loaded structures, provided that the bearing stratum is proven to be consistent and that total and differential settlements are within acceptable limits. However, the presence of the artesian groundwater conditions at Site Alpha, as discussed in Section 4.0, is a controlling factor on the design of any foundation that requires excavation below the existing ground level.

**5.2 Site Alpha – Foundation Design Parameters**

**5.2.1 Piled Foundations**

The preferred foundation solution for Site Alpha is a continuous flight auger (CFA) piled foundation. The piles should be designed to terminate within the underlying chalk, which was encountered at depths of between 4.2 m and 7.8 m below existing ground level across the site. The chalk is considered to provide a suitable bearing stratum, with an allowable base resistance of 1,100 kPa for a pile toe penetration of at least 3 times the pile diameter into the chalk. This value is based on the results of the Standard Penetration Tests (SPT) which recorded N-values of between 18 and 42 in the weathered chalk, and between 45 and refusal in the underlying unweathered chalk.

The shaft resistance within the Head Deposits should be ignored for design purposes, given the variable nature of the material and the potential for softening on exposure to water. The shaft resistance within the weathered chalk may be calculated using the following parameters:

| Parameter | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Adhesion factor (α) | 0.45 |
| Limiting shaft resistance (f_s) | 120 kPa |

The design of the piles must take account of the artesian water conditions. The construction of the piles will be undertaken using a CFA technique, which will limit the open excavation depth and therefore reduce the risk of uncontrolled groundwater inflow. However, the temporary casing must be extended through the Head Deposits and sealed into the top of the chalk to prevent the ingress of water and the softening of the pile toe. The concrete mix should be designed to be suitable for placement in water, and a tremie pipe may be required if water ingress occurs during the concrete pour.

**5.2.2 Bearing Piles – Structural Capacity**

The structural capacity of the piles should be determined by the structural engineer, but it is anticipated that a 600 mm diameter pile will be required to support the typical column loads of 1,200 kN. The pile capacity should be verified by a preliminary pile test and a minimum of two working pile tests, undertaken in accordance with the project specification.

The project team shall be structured to provide clear lines of responsibility and communication. The key roles and responsibilities are defined below:

- **Project Director:** Owns the overall delivery of the project, chairs the PCG, and reports to the Project Board.
- **Project Manager:** Manages the day-to-day delivery, coordinates the Delivery Team, and manages the project controls function.
- **Lead Engineer:** Manages the engineering design, technical assurance, and integration of the design with the construction activities.
- **Construction Manager:** Manages all site-based activities, including health, safety, and environmental (HSE) performance, quality assurance, and the management of the principal contractor.
- **Project Controls Manager:** Manages the planning, cost, and risk functions, providing the data necessary for informed decision-making.
- **Procurement Manager:** Manages all procurement activities, including the tendering and award of subcontracts and the management of the supply chain.

**3.2 Stakeholder Management**

Effective stakeholder engagement is critical to the success of Project X. A Stakeholder Matrix has been developed and is maintained by the PMO, identifying all internal and external stakeholders, their level of interest and influence, and the communication strategy for each. The matrix is reviewed at each PCG meeting.

Key stakeholders include:

- **Sponsoring Organisation:** The parent company funding the project.
- **Client/End Users:** The team who will operate the facility upon completion.
- **Local Authority:** Leeds City Council, with responsibility for planning and building control.
- **Regulatory Bodies:** Environment Agency, Health and Safety Executive (HSE).
- **Local Community:** Residents and businesses adjacent to the Northbridge Industrial Estate.
- **Principal Contractor:** The tier-one contractor responsible for the construction works.
- **Supply Chain:** Subcontractors and material suppliers.

**4. SCOPE MANAGEMENT**

**4.1 Scope Definition**

The scope of Project X is defined in the Project Execution Plan (PEP-PX-003) and the associated technical specifications and drawings. Any work not explicitly defined in these documents is considered to be out of scope.

**4.2 Scope Change Control**

All changes to the project scope shall be managed through the formal Change Control Procedure (see Section 7 of this document). No work outside the defined scope shall be undertaken without an approved Change Request.

**5. SCHEDULE MANAGEMENT**

**5.1 Baseline Schedule**

The project baseline schedule is defined in the Level 3 Programme, reference SCH-PX-004, Revision B. The schedule is based on a contract duration of 35 months, with a planned completion date of 30 November 2027.

Key milestone dates are as follows:

- **Project Start (NTP):** 13 January 2025

- **Construction Start:** 01 September 2025
- **Mechanical Completion:** 30 June 2027
- **Commissioning & Handover:** 30 November 2027

**5.2 Schedule Control**

Progress will be monitored against the baseline schedule on a weekly basis. Earned Value Management (EVM) will be used to measure schedule performance, with Schedule Performance Index (SPI) and Cost Performance Index (CPI) reported to the PCG monthly. Any variance requiring corrective action will be managed through the Risk and Issue Management process.

**7.1 General**

All changes to the project scope, schedule, budget, or quality requirements shall be managed through the Change Control Procedure. The purpose of this procedure is to ensure that all changes are assessed for their impact on the project objectives and that approved changes are implemented in a controlled manner.

**7.2 Change Request Submission**

Any stakeholder, contractor, or member of the project team may submit a Change Request using the standard form (CR-PX-001). The form shall be submitted to the Project Management Office (PMO) for logging and initial review. The Change Request shall include:

- A description of the proposed change.
- The reason for the change.
- An assessment of the impact on scope, schedule, budget, and quality.
- Any supporting documentation, such as drawings, specifications, or quotations.

**7.3 Change Request Review**

The PMO shall review each Change Request within five working days of receipt. The review shall include an assessment of the technical feasibility, the impact on the baseline, and the risks associated with the change. The PMO shall then submit the Change Request to the Change Control Board (CCB) for decision.

**7.4 Change Control Board**

The CCB shall comprise the following members:

- Project Sponsor (Chair)
- Project Director
- Head of Project Controls
- Head of Engineering
- Head of Construction
- Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) Manager

The CCB shall meet on a weekly basis, or more frequently if required, to review and approve or reject Change Requests. The CCB shall consider the impact of each change on the project objectives, the risk profile, and the overall value for money. The decision of the CCB shall be recorded in the minutes of the meeting and communicated to the applicant within two working days.

According to the Project Management Plan, Site Alpha has_planned_completion 2026-03-31. Record status: current.

**7.5 Implementation of Approved Changes**

Once a Change Request has been approved, the PMO shall update the relevant project documentation, including the scope definition, schedule, budget, and risk register. The change shall be communicated to all affected parties, and the project team shall implement the change in accordance with the approved plan. No work shall commence on a change until it has been formally approved by the CCB.

**8. QUALITY MANAGEMENT**

**8.1 Quality Policy**

The quality policy for Project X is to deliver a facility that meets the requirements defined in the technical specifications and the associated British and European standards. The project shall operate a quality management system (QMS) in accordance with ISO 9001:2015, as adapted for the construction industry.

**8.2 Quality Assurance and Quality Control**

Quality assurance (QA) activities shall be undertaken to ensure that the processes used to deliver the project are appropriate and effective. Quality control (QC) activities shall be undertaken to ensure that the products and works meet the specified requirements.

The principal contractor shall be responsible for the development and implementation of a Project Quality Plan (PQP), which shall be submitted to the PMO for approval prior to the commencement of construction works. The PQP shall include:

- The organisational structure and responsibilities for quality.
- Procedures for the control of documents and records.
- Procedures for inspection and testing.
- Procedures for the management of nonconformances.
- Procedures for internal audit.

The PMO shall undertake regular audits of the principal contractor's quality management system and shall monitor the implementation of the PQP throughout the construction phase.

A nonconformance shall be recorded whenever a product, material, or workmanship does not meet the specified requirements. The principal contractor shall maintain a nonconformance register and shall issue a Nonconformance Report (NCR) to the PMO within two working days of identification. Each NCR shall include:

- A unique reference number and the date of identification.
- The location and the relevant work package.
- A description of the nonconformance and the suspected cause.
- The proposed disposition (rework, repair, use-as-is, or reject).
- The signature of the responsible engineer.

The PMO shall review each NCR and shall approve or reject the proposed disposition within five working days. Where the disposition is use-as-is, the PMO shall obtain the written agreement of the client. All costs arising from a nonconformance shall be borne by the party responsible, as determined by the contract.

**8.5 Internal Audit**

documents.content:
**10. Risk Management**

**10.1 Approach**

Risk management for Project X shall be conducted in accordance with the requirements of the Project Risk Management Plan (PRMP-001) and the client's procedures for the management of project risk. The objective of the risk management process is to identify, assess, and manage uncertainties that could affect the delivery of the project objectives, including time, cost, quality, and safety.

The risk management process shall be applied throughout the project lifecycle, from initiation through to close-out. The process shall be proactive, with risks identified and assessed at the earliest opportunity, and shall be reviewed at regular intervals to reflect changes in the project environment.

**10.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

The Project Manager shall have overall accountability for the management of risk on the project. The PMO shall maintain the risk register and shall facilitate the risk review workshops. The principal contractor shall identify and manage risks associated with their scope of work and shall report material risks to the PMO as part of the monthly progress report.

The client's project sponsor shall be responsible for the acceptance of risks that fall outside the tolerance levels set for the project, as described in Section 10.5.

**10.3 Risk Identification and Assessment**

Risks shall be identified through a series of facilitated workshops, interviews, and reviews of project documentation. The initial risk identification shall be undertaken during the development of the Project Execution Plan, and shall be updated at each monthly risk review meeting.

Each risk shall be assessed against two criteria: the likelihood of occurrence and the potential impact on the project objectives. The assessment shall be recorded using the probability-impact matrix shown in Table 10-1.

*Table 10-1: Probability-Impact Matrix*

| Likelihood | Impact | Score | Classification |
|------------|--------|-------|----------------|
| Very Low | Negligible | 1 | Low |
| Low | Minor | 2 | Low |
| Medium | Moderate | 3 | Medium |
| High | Major | 4 | High |
| Very High | Severe | 5 | High |

A risk score shall be calculated by multiplying the likelihood score by the impact score. Risks with a score of 15 or above shall be classified as high risk and shall be subject to active management and mitigation. Risks with a score between 8 and 14 shall be classified as medium risk and shall be managed through the application of standard controls. Risks with a score of 7 or below shall be classified as low risk and shall be monitored through the risk register.

**10.4 Risk Response Planning**

For each risk identified, a response strategy shall be developed. The response strategy shall be selected from the following options:

- Avoid: change the project plan to eliminate the risk or protect the project objectives from its impact.
- Transfer: shift the impact of the risk to a third party, together with ownership of the response.
- Mitigate: reduce the likelihood or impact of the risk to an acceptable level.
- Accept: acknowledge the risk and document its potential impact, with no proactive action taken.

The selected response strategy shall be recorded in the risk register, together with the actions required to implement the response, the owner of the action, and the target date for completion.

**10.5 Risk Tolerances**

The project has the following risk tolerances, which shall be used to determine the level of management action required:

- A risk with a potential cost impact of more than £250,000 shall be escalated to the client's project sponsor for acceptance.
- A risk with a potential schedule impact of more than four weeks to a key milestone shall be escalated to the client's project sponsor for acceptance.
- A risk with a potential impact on the health and safety of personnel or the public shall be escalated to the client's project sponsor immediately.

documents.title: Geotechnical Interpretive Report: Site Alpha and Site Beta
documents.content:
This report presents the factual and interpretive findings of the ground investigation undertaken at Site Alpha and Site Beta between 09 January 2023 and 03 February 2023. It supersedes Revision 0, issued 02 February 2023, which contained preliminary laboratory results only. This revision incorporates the complete suite of geotechnical laboratory testing and is the current controlled document for design purposes.

---

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 This report describes the ground conditions encountered at two adjacent development parcels, Site Alpha (approximately 4.2 ha) and Site Beta (approximately 2.8 ha), located near Didcot, Oxfordshire. The sites are proposed for a mixed-use development comprising residential blocks and light industrial units.

1.2 The investigation was commissioned by Meridian Infrastructure PLC under instruction number MI-4471. The purpose of the investigation was to establish the near-surface ground conditions, groundwater regime, and geotechnical parameters required for foundation design and earthworks specification.

1.3 The scope of work comprised:
- 12 no. rotary cored boreholes (BH01 to BH12)
- 8 no. window sample boreholes (WS01 to WS08)
- 6 no. trial pits (TP01 to TP06)
- In-situ testing including Standard Penetration Tests (SPT) and hand vane tests
- Installation of 4 no. standpipe piezometers
- Geotechnical laboratory testing on recovered samples

1.4 The fieldwork was carried out between 09 January and 03 February 2023. All exploratory hole positions were set out by the site surveyor, and levels were recorded relative to Ordnance Datum (m AOD).

---

2. SITE INVESTIGATION METHODS

2.1 Rotary Core Drilling

2.1.1 Boreholes BH01 to BH12 were advanced using a Dando Terrier 2000 rotary rig equipped with a 112 mm diameter core barrel. Coring was undertaken using a single tube core barrel with a tungsten carbide tipped bit. Flush returns were monitored for the presence of water, and where artesian conditions were suspected, drilling was halted and the hole was observed for a minimum of 30 minutes before continuing.

The Geotechnical Report indicates that Site Alpha has_ground_condition chalk. Record status: current.

2.1.2 Core runs were typically 1.5 m in length, with core recovery and Total Core Recovery (TCR) recorded for each run. Rock Quality Designation (RQD) was calculated for all cored runs within competent strata.

2.1.3 Upon completion of drilling, boreholes were backfilled with cement-bentonite grout, except where piezometers were installed.

2.2 Window Sampling

2.2.1 Window sample boreholes WS01 to WS08 were advanced using a window sampler rig with 1.0 m long, 100 mm diameter sample tubes. Sampling was continuous to refusal or to a maximum depth of 5.0 m.

2.2.2 SPTs were carried out at 1.0 m intervals within the window sample boreholes in accordance with BS EN ISO 22476-3:2005. The SPT hammer was a standard automatic trip hammer with a mass of 63.5 kg and a drop height of 760 mm.

2.3 Trial Pitting

2.3.1 Trial pits TP01 to TP06 were excavated using a 3-tonne mini excavator fitted with a 600 mm toothed bucket. Pits were excavated to a maximum depth of 3.0 m, with side walls inspected and logged by an engineering geologist.

2.3.2 Bulk samples for laboratory classification testing were recovered from each trial pit. In-situ hand vane tests were undertaken at 0.5 m intervals within cohesive horizons.

2.4 Groundwater Monitoring

2.4.1 Four standpipe piezometers were installed in boreholes BH02, BH05, BH08 and BH11. Each piezometer comprised a 50 mm diameter HDPE standpipe with a 1.0 m slotted response zone, surrounded by a sand filter pack and sealed with bentonite.

2.4.2 Groundwater levels were recorded at installation and subsequently on a weekly basis for a period of four weeks. The monitoring period ended on 03 March 2023.

documents.content:
At Site Alpha, the chalk was encountered at depths of between 1.5 m and 3.2 m bgl. The upper 0.5 m to 1.0 m of chalk was typically Grade C, becoming Grade B with increasing depth. In BH05, the chalk was encountered at 2.8 m bgl and was logged as Grade C to a depth of 6.0 m, below which it became Grade B. The chalk at Site Alpha is described in the Geotechnical Report as having a chalk grade of Grade B to C. Record status: current.

At Site Beta, the chalk was encountered at shallower depths, between 1.2 m and 2.5 m bgl. The chalk was generally of better quality than that at Site Alpha, with Grade B material recorded from the top of the chalk in BH11 and BH12. In BH13, a band of harder, Grade A chalk was recorded between 4.5 m and 5.2 m bgl.

3.5 Groundwater

3.5.1 General

Groundwater levels were recorded in the standpipe piezometers installed in BH02, BH05, BH08 and BH11 during the monitoring period between 03 February 2023 and 03 March 2023. The recorded levels are presented in Table 3.1 below. It should be noted that the monitoring period was relatively short, and that groundwater levels may vary seasonally.

Table 3.1: Groundwater levels recorded during monitoring period

Borehole | Depth to water (m bgl) | Date of reading | Notes
BH02 | 2.1 | 03 Feb 2023 | Falling
BH02 | 2.4 | 10 Feb 2023 | Falling
BH02 | 2.5 | 03 Mar 2023 | Stable
BH05 | 3.0 | 03 Feb 2023 | Rising
BH05 | 2.8 | 10 Feb 2023 | Rising
BH05 | 2.6 | 03 Mar 2023 | Stable
BH08 | 1.5 | 03 Feb 2023 | Stable
BH08 | 1.5 | 03 Mar 2023 | Stable
BH11 | 1.8 | 03 Feb 2023 | Stable
BH11 | 1.8 | 03 Mar 2023 | Stable

3.5.2 Artesian Conditions at Site Alpha

During drilling of borehole BH05 at Site Alpha, artesian water conditions were encountered. Upon completion of drilling to the full depth of 12.0 m, the borehole was observed to be flowing with water at a rate sufficient to maintain a standing water level above the ground surface. The flow was estimated at approximately 0.5 litres per second. A period of observation of 30 minutes was undertaken, during which the flow continued unabated. The artesian head was measured using a temporary standpipe and pressure gauge, which recorded a pressure equivalent to a water level of approximately 1.2 m above ground level.

The Geotechnical Report notes that Site Alpha has_ground_condition artesian water. Record status: current.

The artesian conditions are interpreted to be associated with a confined chalk aquifer beneath the site. The Head Deposits and the upper weathered chalk are considered to act as an aquitard, confining the groundwater within the more fractured and permeable chalk at depth. The artesian head is considered to be a result of the regional topography, with recharge occurring at higher elevations to the north of the site and the confined aquifer transmitting water beneath the site towards the river valley to the south.

The presence of artesian water has significant implications for the design and construction of the proposed development at Site Alpha. In particular, any excavation that penetrates the confining layer will be subject to groundwater inflow from below, which may be difficult to control. It is recommended that the following measures are considered during detailed design:

1. A full pumping test should be undertaken to determine the transmissivity and storage coefficient of the chalk aquifer, and to assess the sustainability of any dewatering scheme.

2. The design of the basement and any deep drainage should take account of the artesian head, and should incorporate appropriate pressure relief measures, such as pressure relief valves or a permanent dewatering system.

3. A permit to work should be required for any excavation that is expected to penetrate the confining layer, and a contingency plan should be in place for dealing with uncontrolled groundwater inflows.

**Geotechnical Interpretive Report: Site Alpha and Site Beta**
**Document Reference: GIR-2026-014**
**Revision: C (Final for Detailed Design)**

**5.0 Recommendations for Foundation Design**

The following recommendations are made for the design of foundations for the proposed development at Site Alpha and Site Beta. These recommendations are based on the findings of the intrusive investigation, laboratory testing, and the geological model presented in Sections 2.0 to 4.0 of this report. The recommendations are made on the basis of the assumed development layout and loading, as provided by the project architects and structural engineers. Should the layout or loading change significantly, the recommendations should be reviewed.

**5.1 General**

The ground conditions across both sites are variable, and it is therefore essential that a rigorous approach to foundation design is adopted. A traditional strip or pad foundation solution is not considered appropriate for the majority of the development, due to the presence of soft, compressible Head Deposits and the potential for differential settlement. A piled foundation solution, or a ground improvement scheme, is considered necessary to transfer loads to the more competent strata.

The use of a reinforced concrete raft foundation may be considered for lightly loaded structures, provided that the bearing stratum is proven to be consistent and that total and differential settlements are within acceptable limits. However, the presence of the artesian groundwater conditions at Site Alpha, as discussed in Section 4.0, is a controlling factor on the design of any foundation that requires excavation below the existing ground level.

**5.2 Site Alpha – Foundation Design Parameters**

**5.2.1 Piled Foundations**

The preferred foundation solution for Site Alpha is a continuous flight auger (CFA) piled foundation. The piles should be designed to terminate within the underlying chalk, which was encountered at depths of between 4.2 m and 7.8 m below existing ground level across the site. The chalk is considered to provide a suitable bearing stratum, with an allowable base resistance of 1,100 kPa for a pile toe penetration of at least 3 times the pile diameter into the chalk. This value is based on the results of the Standard Penetration Tests (SPT) which recorded N-values of between 18 and 42 in the weathered chalk, and between 45 and refusal in the underlying unweathered chalk.

The shaft resistance within the Head Deposits should be ignored for design purposes, given the variable nature of the material and the potential for softening on exposure to water. The shaft resistance within the weathered chalk may be calculated using the following parameters:

| Parameter | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Adhesion factor (α) | 0.45 |
| Limiting shaft resistance (f_s) | 120 kPa |

The design of the piles must take account of the artesian water conditions. The construction of the piles will be undertaken using a CFA technique, which will limit the open excavation depth and therefore reduce the risk of uncontrolled groundwater inflow. However, the temporary casing must be extended through the Head Deposits and sealed into the top of the chalk to prevent the ingress of water and the softening of the pile toe. The concrete mix should be designed to be suitable for placement in water, and a tremie pipe may be required if water ingress occurs during the concrete pour.

**5.2.2 Bearing Piles – Structural Capacity**

The structural capacity of the piles should be determined by the structural engineer, but it is anticipated that a 600 mm diameter pile will be required to support the typical column loads of 1,200 kN. The pile capacity should be verified by a preliminary pile test and a minimum of two working pile tests, undertaken in accordance with the project specification.

**1. Equipment Availability Summary (May – December 2026)**

The following table summarises the availability of all plant items logged in this register during the reporting period. Availability is calculated as (hours available for work ÷ total hours in period) × 100, excluding planned downtime for servicing and statutory inspections.

---

**2. Significant Maintenance Events and Repairs (May – December 2026)**

This section records all non-routine maintenance activities, repairs, and inspections that affected equipment availability or required escalation. Entries are listed in chronological order.

**2.1 PUMP-01 – Unplanned Repair (22 May 2026)**

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Date reported | 22 May 2026, 09:15 BST |
| Equipment ID | PUMP-01 |
| Fault description | Pump losing prime intermittently; discharge pressure fluctuating between 2.1 and 3.4 bar. |
| Action taken | Strip-down inspection of impeller and wear rings. Found debris (small aggregate) lodged between impeller vanes. Impeller cleaned; wear ring replaced (part no. WR-221). |
| Parts used | Wear ring WR-221 (1 off), gasket set GS-114 (1 off) |
| Labour | P. Doyle (2 h), R. Hussain (2 h) |
| Downtime | 14 hours (09:30–23:30) |
| Root cause | Inlet strainer had a split mesh, allowing aggregate to pass. Strainer replaced (part no. ST-308). |
| Follow-up | Weekly inspection of strainer condition added to maintenance schedule. |
| Cost | £184.50 (parts), £96.00 (labour) |

**2.2 GEN-01 – Coolant Leak Investigation (14 June 2026)**

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Date reported | 14 June 2026, 14:00 BST |
| Equipment ID | GEN-01 |
| Fault description | Operator reported small puddle of coolant beneath radiator. |
| Action taken | Pressure test of cooling system. Found leak at bottom hose connection – clamp had worked loose. Hose refitted and new clamp fitted (part no. CL-118). |
| Labour | A. Okafor (1 h) |
| Downtime | 2 hours (14:30–16:30) |
| Root cause | Vibration from continuous running had loosened the original clamp. |
| Follow-up | Torque check on all coolant clamps added to the 500-hour service checklist. |
| Cost | £4.80 (clamp), £32.00 (labour) |
